baselineReaders.essens: The reader is an experienced developer who wants to understand quickly why this code is here, what main work happens, and which decisive conditions or consequences an accurate main picture needs. Choose a higher level of abstraction: say what a mechanism achieves and what follows from it for the main behaviour, not the calls, state flags, loop steps, types, queues or guards that achieve it; this reader reads the ordinary mechanics in the code. Brevity comes from meaningful selection, not from packing the same details into fewer sentences. A detail belongs in the first part when the main behaviour needs it or leaving it out would mislead; further mechanics this reader may want next go after the marker, or stay in the step that treats them.
baselineReaders.standard: The reader knows programming but not this code: make the central mechanism understandable, how the parts work together and why their relationship matters, from a natural entry point into what makes the behaviour understandable rather than the parts in source order. Place a project-specific name the first time it matters, and explain a language detail where the reader needs it to interpret the code; you need not teach every concept, nor add facts to be longer.
baselineReaders.pedagog: The reader can program but may not know this language, library or mechanism: build the understanding the reasoning presupposes, what the concepts mean here, why the mechanism is needed and how the parts work together, and tie it to what the code does here, with a concrete example or comparison where it makes the reasoning easier to follow. Choose the concepts and intermediate steps this step actually needs: do not inventory every line or teach every term, and do not add facts to be longer than Standard. Use what the walk has established: a short reminder with a reference in a later step, not the same foundation derived again. State what a primitive guarantees before an argument rests on it, and name a fault for what it is: unsynchronised concurrent access with a writer is a data race, not a stale value. A local explanation beats a detached lesson, and the text may take the room understanding needs.

variantReaders.essens: The reader is an experienced developer who wants to orient quickly. Organise the explanation around what this code is for and its most important effect in the flow: summarise several code operations into one meaningful action that helps this reader orient, rather than going through the operations; this reader reads the ordinary mechanics in the code. When the reader understands the step's task, its connection to the flow and the decisive consequence, the base explanation is done; further relevant facts are not automatically further things to tell here. A detail belongs in the first part when the main picture would otherwise mislead; mechanics this reader may want next go after the marker, or stay in the step that treats them. What the walk has already established need not be repeated, and more complex code may need more room.
variantReaders.standard: The reader knows programming but not this code. Organise the explanation around how the central mechanism achieves the effect and how the parts work together, from a natural entry point rather than the parts in source order. The base explanation is done when the central mechanism is understandable; it does not go on through the rest of the surroundings. Place a project-specific name the first time it matters, and explain a language detail where the reader needs it to interpret the code; you need not teach every concept, nor add facts to be longer.
variantReaders.pedagog: The reader can program but may not know this language, library or mechanism. Organise the explanation around the understanding this reader must build to grasp the mechanism: the concepts it rests on, the intermediate steps and, where it helps, a concrete example or comparison, tied to what the code does here. Develop the concepts that understanding needs and no others: do not inventory every line or teach every term, and do not add facts to be longer than Standard. Use what the walk has established: a short reminder with a reference in a later step, not the same foundation derived again. State what a primitive guarantees before an argument rests on it, and name a fault for what it is: unsynchronised concurrent access with a writer is a data race, not a stale value. A local explanation beats a detached lesson, and the text may take the room understanding needs.

sharedScopeRule: Let the scope follow the code and the reader: a simple step is said in a few words in every profile, and a step where several mechanisms interact takes the room understanding needs. There is no length to hit and no required form; use a paragraph, a list or a small code excerpt where it helps, and let every sentence add understanding. Point at the code you rest on with references, so the person can open it.
addedToSharedScopeRule: These are the reader's perspective, not headings or a checklist, and the same facts may appear in several profiles; no profile goes on only because the material holds more facts.
